Short [mɛn], the stressed second syllable of the name.
Short [ti.a], the abstract-noun ending that gives clementia its meaning.

pronunciation.approximation: 'kleh-MEN-tee-ah' — stress the second syllable; all vowels are short in Classical Latin.
pronunciation.note: Clementia is a Latin word and concept. It has no 'original script' other than the Latin alphabet. The ASCII form clementia is already the Latin spelling; the restoration capitalises the proper-noun form. Because no distinctive diacritic or special letter is added, the entry is Tier 2.

domains.title: Mercy and Clemency
domains.subtitle: The Virtue of Restrained Power
domains.lead: Clementia is the Roman personification and virtue of mercy, mildness, and clemency. She represents the deliberate restraint of power: the emperor who pardons a defeated enemy, the judge who tempers justice with compassion, the victor who refuses to humiliate the vanquished. In a culture that valued severity and strength, Clementia named the rare and admirable quality of showing mercy without weakness.

cards.name: Mercy
cards.desc: The willingness to spare those who have done wrong or been defeated.

cards.name: Clemency
cards.desc: The moderation of punishment by those who have the power to punish severely.

cards.name: Forgiveness
cards.desc: The release of a debtor or offender from the full weight of their debt.

cards.name: Restrained Power
cards.desc: The distinctive Roman idea that mercy is most virtuous when power is greatest.

symbols.name: Olive branch
symbols.meaning: The universal sign of peace and the offer of mercy.

symbols.name: Patera
symbols.meaning: The sacrificial bowl from which mercy is poured as a libation.

symbols.name: Kneeling suppliant
symbols.meaning: The figure who receives clemency, emphasising the power differential mercy bridges.

symbols.name: Cornucopia
symbols.meaning: The abundance that flows from a rule that is just but not cruel.

mythology.lead: Clementia is not a narrative goddess with a family tree of myths; she is a personified virtue whose 'mythology' is the history of Roman political ethics. Her story is told in senatorial debates, imperial propaganda, and the coins on which emperors advertised their mercy to the empire.

myths.title: The Clemency of Caesar
myths.text: Julius Caesar made clementia a central virtue of his public image. After defeating his enemies in the civil war, he famously pardoned many of them, including Brutus and Cicero. The temple of Clementia was vowed in his honour. Caesar's clemency was praised by some as magnanimity and denounced by others as calculated domination — the mercy of a man who could afford to be merciful.

myths.title: Clementia Augusti
myths.text: Under the empire, Clementia became an official virtue of the emperor. Coins and inscriptions proclaimed the *Clementia Augusti*, the mercy of Augustus and his successors. The virtue served both as a moral ideal and as propaganda: the emperor was powerful enough to destroy his enemies but chose to spare them.

myths.title: On Clemency
myths.text: Seneca wrote his *De Clementia* for the young emperor Nero, arguing that clemency is the most becoming virtue of a ruler. True clemency, he insists, is not weakness but the restrained use of absolute power. The treatise is at once a philosophical essay and a work of political advice, warning Nero that cruelty destroys the very security it seeks to protect.

myths.title: Mercy and the Divine
myths.text: Christian Latin adopted clementia as a name for God's mercy toward sinners. The word appears in hymns, prayers, and theological treatises, where it translates Greek eleos and Hebrew hesed. Clementia thus moved from imperial ideology to devotional language, retaining its sense of unmerited compassion shown by one who has power to punish.

syncretism: The Roman Clementia overlaps with Greek Praotes (gentleness) and Eleos (mercy). She also resembles the Christian virtue of misericordia. In political theory, the concept of clemency runs from Seneca through Machiavelli — who warned princes that mercy could be dangerous — to modern discussions of presidential pardons and transitional justice. The word 'clemency' survives in legal English, though the personified goddess has faded from public memory.
culturalLegacy: Clementia remains a living concept in law and politics. Executive clemency, the power to pardon or commute sentences, is one of the oldest prerogatives of rulers. The debate Seneca began — whether mercy strengthens or weakens authority — still shapes arguments about criminal justice, amnesty, and political reconciliation. In an age of mass incarceration and polarised politics, Clementia asks whether the powerful can afford to be merciful and whether the powerless can afford to hope for mercy.
extendedMeditation:
Clementia is the virtue of those who have power and choose not to use all of it. That choice is harder than it sounds, because power tends to justify its own extremes. To show mercy is to acknowledge that the person before you is more than their offence, more than their defeat, more than their debt.

Yet Clementia is not sentimental. Seneca knew that mercy must be guided by justice, or it becomes licence. The ideal is not softness but strength directed toward the common good. In a world that often mistakes cruelty for clarity, Clementia reminds us that restraint can be the deepest form of power.
originalScriptNote: Clementia is a Latin word. Its canonical form is the Latin spelling clementia. The ASCII form clementia already represents the Latin spelling exactly. The restoration Clementia is therefore the capitalised proper-noun citation form, not a phonetic recovery. The appropriate label is 'Latin' or 'Scholarly Transliteration'.
